glossary.definition: Diffraction is the spatial spreading and interference of a wave after an aperture or obstacle restricts its wavefront.
Fraunhofer diffraction is the far-field angular diffraction pattern, or the equivalent pattern formed in a lens focal plane. The aperture's quadratic propagation phase can be neglected.
Fresnel diffraction is near-field diffraction in which the curvature of propagation phase across an aperture must be retained.
A phasor is a complex number representing the amplitude and phase of a sinusoidal wave. Adding phasors accounts for interference.
Coherent waves have a stable phase relationship over the observation time, allowing a steady interference pattern.
An envelope is a slowly varying boundary or modulation of a more rapidly varying pattern. Single-slit diffraction modulates the rapid double-slit interference fringes.
A missing order is an interference principal maximum that disappears because it falls at a zero of the individual-slit diffraction factor.
A diffraction grating is an array of regularly spaced slits or grooves that produces sharp interference maxima at selected directions.
Resolving power is the ability to distinguish two nearby spectral wavelengths, quantified by wavelength divided by the smallest resolvable wavelength separation.
Angular dispersion of a grating is the rate at which its diffraction angle changes with wavelength, at a fixed diffraction order.

A Fresnel half-period zone is a region of a wavefront whose paths to an observation point differ by less than half a wavelength, with successive zone boundaries separated by a half-wavelength path increment.
A zone plate is a diffractive focusing element made of concentric rings that transmit alternate Fresnel zones or change their phases so their contributions reinforce at a focus.

Cornu’s spiral is the parametric curve with coordinates given by the two Fresnel integrals. A chord between two points represents the resultant field from the corresponding interval of a diffracting aperture.
Polarization describes the motion of the electric-field vector in the plane transverse to a light wave's travel. Linear polarization confines it to one fixed line.
A polarizer is an optical element that selects a polarization component from incident light.
An analyser is a polarizing element used to test the polarization of light, usually by rotating its transmission axis.
The Rayleigh criterion calls two equal spectral peaks just resolved when the principal maximum of one coincides with the nearest minimum of the other.
A transverse wave oscillates perpendicular to its direction of travel. For light, polarization concerns the transverse electric field.

cards.title: Question 1
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Explain physically, by dividing the slit into two equal halves, why the first minimum in a single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern occurs at \(b\sin\theta=\lambda\).
cards.recallAnswer: Divide the uniformly illuminated slit into two halves and pair each point in one half with the point b/2 away in the other. At \(b\sin\theta=\lambda\), each pair has path difference \((b/2)\sin\theta=\lambda/2\) and phase difference π. Equal paired contributions cancel, giving the first minimum on either side of the centre.

cards.q: Did you describe the half-slit pairing and its path difference?

options.t: Pairs separated by \(b/2\), giving \((b/2)\sin\theta\)
Divided the slit but pairing or geometry incomplete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Pairing must cancel the whole slit, not just its edge rays.

cards.q: Did you connect a half-wavelength difference to complete cancellation?

options.t: Phase \(\pi\), equal amplitudes cancel; \(b\sin\theta=\lambda\)
First-minimum equation quoted without the reason
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: At the centre the path difference is zero, so the central peak is not a minimum.

cards.title: Pair every point, not only the edges
cards.body: Join each point in the upper half to the corresponding point in the lower half. Their separation is b/2, so every pair cancels in the first-minimum direction.

cards.title: Remember
points: Split the aperture into two equal halves.
Pair contributions separated by b/2.
The first minimum is caused by pairwise destructive interference.

cards.q: The slit is divided into equal ____ for the first-minimum argument.
cards.why: Each half provides a matching partner for every contribution in the other.

cards.q: Each pair cancels through ____ interference.
cards.why: The paired contributions differ in phase by π.

cards.q: The central direction is a ____, not the first minimum.
cards.why: All aperture contributions have equal phase at θ = 0.

cards.title: Question 2
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Give the expression for the intensity distribution in a two-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and explain the physical significance of the two factors involved. What happens when the slit width \(b\) becomes very small?
cards.recallAnswer: For centre separation d, \(I=4I_s(\sin\beta/\beta)^2\cos^2\gamma\), with \(\beta=\pi b\sin\theta/\lambda\) and \(\gamma=\pi d\sin\theta/\lambda\). The sinc-squared factor is the single-slit diffraction envelope; cosine-squared gives interference between the slits. For very narrow slits the envelope is broad and nearly constant over the fringes (normalized angular pattern).

cards.q: Did you write the distribution and define β and γ consistently?

options.t: Both factors and b/d definitions correct
Correct structure but incomplete parameters or normalization
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: I_s is the on-axis intensity from one slit alone.

cards.q: Did you explain both factors and the narrow-slit limit?

options.t: Envelope versus fringes, with broad nearly constant envelope for narrow b
Only one factor explained
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Narrowing a slit broadens its angular diffraction envelope; it also reduces transmitted power if illumination is fixed.

cards.title: Envelope times interference
cards.body: The narrow-slit statement concerns the normalized shape. It does not assert that finite intensity remains when a physical aperture shrinks to zero width.

cards.title: Remember
points: b is slit width; d is centre-to-centre spacing.
Diffraction provides the broad envelope.
Two-slit interference supplies rapid fringes within that envelope.

cards.q: The single-slit factor supplies the diffraction ____.
cards.why: It modulates the rapid two-slit fringes.

cards.q: The cosine-squared factor describes two-slit ____.
cards.why: It comes from adding the two slit fields.

cards.q: Making the slits narrower makes their angular envelope ____.
cards.why: Its first zero satisfies sinθ = λ/b.

cards.title: Question 3
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: What do you mean by missing orders in a double-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern? State the condition under which a particular interference maximum is absent.
cards.recallAnswer: A missing order is a two-slit interference maximum erased by a zero of the single-slit envelope. Both \(d\sin\theta=m\lambda\) and \(b\sin\theta=p\lambda\) must hold, with nonzero integer p. Thus \(mb=pd\), or \(m=pd/b\). If d/b is an integer q, every qth nonzero interference order is absent.

cards.q: Did you define the phenomenon and give both coincident conditions?

options.t: An interference maximum at a diffraction zero, with both equations
Definition or only one condition correct
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The central order is not missing: the envelope has a limiting maximum there.

cards.q: Did you derive the order relation and specify nonzero diffraction order?

options.t: \(mb=pd\) with \(p\ne0\), and correct integer-ratio example
Relation correct but order qualification absent
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: For \(d/b=3\), interference orders \(\pm3,\pm6,\ldots\) are absent.

cards.title: A concrete missing order
cards.body: The interference factor alone predicts a bright third order, but the diffraction factor is zero there.

cards.title: Remember
points: A missing order needs simultaneous maximum and envelope-zero conditions.
Use centre spacing d, not opaque-gap width.
Do not include p = 0 as a diffraction minimum.

cards.q: A missing interference order lies at an envelope ____.
cards.why: The single-slit intensity factor is zero there.

cards.q: The spacing d refers to slit ____.
cards.why: The phase difference uses centre-to-centre separation.

cards.q: The central interference order remains ____.
cards.why: sinβ/β tends to one at β = 0.

cards.title: Question 4
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Give the grating equation and explain why no dispersion occurs in the zeroth-order spectrum. What is meant by overlapping of spectra in a diffraction grating?
cards.recallAnswer: At normal incidence the principal maxima satisfy \(d\sin\theta=m\lambda\), where d is grating spacing. For m=0 all wavelengths go along θ=0, so no wavelength separation occurs. Spectra overlap when different orders of different wavelengths have the same angle: \(m\lambda=m'\lambda'\).

cards.q: Did you give the grating equation, symbols and zeroth-order explanation?

options.t: \(d\sin\theta=m\lambda\) with symbols; all wavelengths at zero angle for \(m=0\)
Only the equation or zeroth-order explanation complete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The statement assumes normal incidence.

cards.q: Did you explain spectral overlap with its condition?

options.t: Different wavelengths/orders share an angle when \(m\lambda=m'\lambda'\)
Qualitative overlap without the condition
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The grating selects the product of order and wavelength.

cards.title: Zero order has no angular dispersion
cards.body: For example, a second-order 400 nm line and a first-order 800 nm line overlap if both orders are allowed.

cards.title: Remember
points: State normal incidence for the simple grating equation.
Zero order has no wavelength separation.
Different orders can superpose at equal mλ.

cards.q: The zeroth-order beam has no angular ____.
cards.why: Its diffraction angle is independent of wavelength.

cards.q: Spectral overlap may involve different diffraction ____.
cards.why: Different m values can compensate different wavelengths.

cards.q: The simple equation in this answer assumes ____ incidence.
cards.why: Oblique incidence introduces the incidence-angle term.

cards.title: Question 5
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: What do you mean by the resolving power of a grating? Give an expression for the same explaining the terms involved.
cards.recallAnswer: The resolving power is \(\mathcal R=\lambda/\Delta\lambda\), where Δλ is the smallest wavelength difference just distinguishable near λ. By the Rayleigh criterion for an ideal uniformly illuminated grating, \(\mathcal R=|m|N\), where m is diffraction order and N is the total number of illuminated rulings (not the line density).

cards.q: Did you define spectral resolving power and its wavelength ratio?

options.t: Ability to distinguish close wavelengths; \(\lambda/\Delta\lambda\) with \(\Delta\lambda\) identified
Only qualitative definition or ratio correct
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Resolving power is distinct from angular dispersion.

cards.q: Did you give \(|m|N\) and define N correctly?

options.t: \(|m|N\); \(N\) is total illuminated slits/rulings
Formula right but N confused with line density
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A wider illuminated region can improve resolution even at fixed line density.

cards.title: Total lines, not lines per length
cards.body: The ideal result uses the Rayleigh criterion and equal, coherent illumination. It does not imply useful spectral resolution in zero order.

cards.title: Remember
points: Resolution asks whether two nearby wavelengths can be distinguished.
Dispersion asks how much their angles differ.
Use the total illuminated number of rulings.

cards.q: Resolving power describes the ability to distinguish close ____.
cards.why: Its definition compares λ with the smallest distinguishable Δλ.

cards.q: N counts the total ____ rulings.
cards.why: Rulings outside the illuminated width do not sharpen this pattern.

cards.q: The ideal grating resolution formula uses the ____ criterion.
cards.why: A maximum of one line coincides with a nearby minimum of the other.

sheets.title: Q6 · Near field and zone areas

cards.title: Question 6
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: How does Fresnel diffraction differ from Fraunhofer diffraction? For a plane wavefront of monochromatic light, what is the difference in areas of the \(n^{\mathrm{th}}\) and \((n-1)^{\mathrm{th}}\) Fresnel half-period zones?
cards.recallAnswer: Fresnel diffraction retains wavefront/propagation curvature at finite distance; Fraunhofer is the far-field angular pattern or its lens focal-plane equivalent. For a plane wavefront with observation distance D, the paraxial zone areas are all approximately \(\pi\lambda D\), so adjacent areas differ by approximately zero. Retaining the small exact spherical-distance correction gives \(A_n-A_{n-1}=\pi\lambda^2/2\) for n≥2.

cards.q: Did you contrast the two diffraction regimes?

options.t: Near-field curvature versus far-field/focal-plane angular pattern
Finite versus effectively infinite distance without phase explanation
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A lens can form a Fraunhofer pattern at a finite screen distance.

cards.q: Did you state the equal-zone-area approximation and its difference?

options.t: Each area \(\approx\pi\lambda D\), so adjacent difference \(\approx0\); exact correction accepted
Equal areas stated without identifying the approximation
Confused zone area with cumulative disk area

cards.why: The nth disk grows with n, but an individual half-period zone is an annulus.

cards.title: Annulus area versus disk area
cards.body: Neglecting the λ² correction gives the textbook equal-area result. Exact adjacent zone areas differ by πλ²/2, tiny compared with πλD.

cards.title: Remember
points: Fresnel retains quadratic phase across the aperture.
Fraunhofer is a far-field or focal-plane pattern.
Individual plane-wave half-period zones have approximately equal areas.

cards.q: The Fresnel regime retains propagation-phase ____.
cards.why: Finite-distance path differences include a quadratic aperture-coordinate term.

cards.q: An individual outer half-period zone is an ____.
cards.why: It lies between consecutive circular boundaries.

cards.q: In the paraxial approximation these zone areas are ____.
cards.why: The difference of successive squared radii is λD.

cards.title: Question 7
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Write down the equation for the principal focal length of a zone plate. Compare a zone plate and a convex lens.
cards.recallAnswer: For plane-wave illumination in the paraxial approximation, \(f_1=r_1^2/\lambda=r_n^2/(n\lambda)\). A zone plate focuses by diffraction through alternate zones; a convex lens focuses by refraction. A binary amplitude zone plate has real positive foci \(f_1,f_1/3,f_1/5,\ldots\), unlike the single principal paraxial focus of an ideal simple lens at a fixed wavelength. Its principal f varies inversely with λ.

cards.q: Did you give the principal focal-length formula and define the radii?

options.t: \(f_1=r_1^2/\lambda=r_n^2/(n\lambda)\), with zone-boundary radii identified
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: \(r_n\) is the nth zone boundary, not an annulus width.

cards.q: Did you make at least two valid comparisons?

options.t: Diffraction/refraction and multiple/single principal focus, or correct wavelength contrast
Only one sound comparison
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The ordinary amplitude plate's converging secondary foci occur at odd orders.

cards.title: Odd-order converging foci
cards.body: This answer concerns a conventional binary amplitude zone plate. Its chromatic dependence is much stronger than that of an ordinary refracting lens.

cards.title: Remember
points: Zone plates focus by diffraction.
Their radii follow a square-root sequence.
A conventional amplitude plate has multiple odd-order positive foci.

cards.q: A zone plate focuses light by ____.
cards.why: Transmitted zone contributions interfere constructively.

cards.q: A simple convex glass lens focuses chiefly by ____.
cards.why: Its surfaces change the propagation direction through refraction.

cards.q: The positive secondary zone-plate foci correspond to ____ orders.
cards.why: An ideal alternating amplitude pattern suppresses the even diffraction orders.

cards.title: Question 8
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Define the Fresnel integrals \(C(\tau)\) and \(S(\tau)\) and state their basic properties. What is Cornu’s spiral?
cards.recallAnswer: \(C(\tau)=\int_0^\tau\cos(\pi u^2/2)\,du\) and \(S(\tau)=\int_0^\tau\sin(\pi u^2/2)\,du\). Both are odd and vanish at zero; each tends to 1/2 at +∞ and −1/2 at −∞. Cornu’s spiral is the parametric curve (C(τ),S(τ)); a chord represents the complex field from the corresponding aperture interval.

cards.q: Did you write both integrals with the correct phase and limits?

options.t: Both integrals from zero to \(\tau\), with \(\pi u^2/2\) in cosine and sine
One integral correct or minor normalization error
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Different conventions rescale the variable; use one consistently.

cards.q: Did you state properties and identify Cornu’s spiral?

options.t: Oddness, zero values, ±½ limits and the (C,S) parametric curve
Only properties or curve identification complete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The spiral ends approach (½,½) and (−½,−½).

cards.title: The paired integrals
cards.body: Odd functions can have oscillatory approaches to their limits; neither Fresnel integral is globally monotone.

cards.title: Remember
points: Use πu²/2 consistently.
Both functions are odd.
Cornu coordinates are C and S; field sums are represented by chords.

cards.q: Both Fresnel integral functions are ____.
cards.why: Their integrands are even, but integrating from zero makes each integral odd.

cards.q: Cornu’s spiral is a ____ curve.
cards.why: The parameter τ determines both C and S.

cards.q: A Cornu-spiral chord represents a resultant wave ____.
cards.why: Its two components are the real and imaginary diffraction integrals.

cards.title: Question 9
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Define polarization of light. Distinguish between unpolarized, linearly polarized, and circularly polarized waves.
cards.recallAnswer: Polarization describes the electric-field vector's motion transverse to propagation. In unpolarized light its transverse direction fluctuates irregularly in time. For linear polarization the vector oscillates on a fixed line. For circular polarization it rotates with constant magnitude: two perpendicular equal-amplitude components have a ±π/2 phase difference.

cards.q: Did you define polarization and distinguish unpolarized from linear light?

options.t: Electric-field transverse motion; irregular directions versus a fixed line
Only definition or one state is complete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Unpolarized light is not a single fixed circular or linear state.

cards.q: Did you state the circular-polarization conditions?

options.t: Equal orthogonal components in quadrature; constant-length rotation
Rotation stated without its component conditions
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Unequal quadrature components give an ellipse, not a circle.

cards.title: Watch one point in space
cards.body: Observe the electric-field tip at a fixed point over time: a line for linear polarization, a circle for circular polarization, and irregular motion for unpolarized light.

cards.title: Remember
points: Polarization concerns the transverse electric field.
Linear means fixed oscillation direction.
Circular requires equal orthogonal amplitudes and a quarter-cycle phase difference.

cards.q: Linear polarization keeps the electric-field direction ____.
cards.why: The vector changes sign on one line, rather than changing the line itself.

cards.q: Circular polarization requires equal orthogonal component ____.
cards.why: Equal amplitudes and quadrature produce a circle.

cards.q: The transverse direction in unpolarized light fluctuates ____.
cards.why: It lacks a stable polarization direction over the observation time.

cards.title: Question 10
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Write down the expressions for the electric and magnetic field vectors \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf H\) of a linearly polarized plane wave propagating along the \(z\)-direction in a dielectric. Define polarizer and analyser.
cards.recallAnswer: In a homogeneous isotropic lossless dielectric choose \(\mathbf E=\hat x E_0\cos(\omega t-kz)\), \(\mathbf H=\hat y(E_0/\eta)\cos(\omega t-kz)\), with \(\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}\), \(k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}\). E and H are in phase and E×H points along +z. A polarizer selects a polarization component; an analyser tests the emerging polarization.

cards.q: Did you write compatible vector fields and the amplitude relation?

options.t: Perpendicular in-phase \(\mathbf E,\mathbf H\), correct \(+z\) phase and \(H_0=E_0/\eta\)
Directions or amplitudes incomplete but propagation is consistent
Missing or inconsistent

cards.why: H is magnetic-field strength; \(\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H\) is a different field quantity.

cards.q: Did you define both optical elements?

options.t: Polarizer selects, analyser tests polarization
Only one role correctly defined
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The same type of element can serve either role depending on its position and purpose.

cards.title: Right-handed field directions
cards.tex: \mathbf E\perp\mathbf H\perp\hat z,\qquad \mathbf E\times\mathbf H\parallel+\hat z,\qquad \frac{E_0}{H_0}=\sqrt{\frac\mu\varepsilon}
cards.body: The perpendicularity statement means both fields are perpendicular to propagation and to each other. Do not replace H₀ with B₀ in the amplitude ratio.

cards.title: Remember
points: Specify a lossless dielectric for the in-phase field expressions.
Use H₀ = E₀/η and B = μH.
A polarizer prepares; an analyser tests.

cards.q: A polarizer ____ a polarization component.
cards.why: It transmits a selected component of the electric field.

cards.q: An analyser is used to ____ polarization.
cards.why: Its transmitted intensity changes as its axis is rotated relative to the incident state.

cards.q: In the stated lossless dielectric, E and H are in ____.
cards.why: Their sinusoidal factors have the same phase.

cards.title: Question 11
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: A parallel beam of light of wavelength \(\lambda=5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}\) is incident normally on a narrow slit of width \(0.2\,\mathrm{mm}\). The Fraunhofer diffraction pattern is observed on a screen placed at the focal plane of a convex lens of focal length \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\) placed close to the slit. Calculate the distance between the first two minima and the first two secondary maxima on the screen.
Did you convert the data and state which pair of positions you are comparing?

options.t: λ = 500 nm, b = 0.2 mm, f = 0.2 m; opposite-side or same-side convention explicit
Conversions correct but pair convention unstated
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The wording can mean the nearest symmetric pair or the first and second positions on one side.

cards.q: Did you find and compare the minima consistently?

options.t: Positions ±0.500 mm: symmetric separation 1.000 mm; or same-side 0.500 and 1.000 mm giving 0.500 mm
Correct minimum formula with a calculation error
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Paraxially y_m = mfλ/b.

cards.q: Did you locate secondary maxima using a stated approximation?

options.t: \(\tan\beta=\beta\) roots give symmetric 1.430 mm or same-side 0.514 mm; consistent textbook half-integer approximation also credited
Correct maximum method but incomplete roots or separation
Used minima as secondary maxima

cards.why: The first exact roots are 4.4934 and 7.7253, not \(3\pi/2\) and \(5\pi/2\) exactly.

cards.title: First locate, then subtract
cards.body: The two minima flanking the central maximum are −0.500 and +0.500 mm, separated by 1.000 mm. The first two on one side are separated by 0.500 mm.

cards.title: Exact stationary roots, paraxial screen
cards.body: The first positive secondary maxima are at 0.71515 and 1.22951 mm. Opposite first maxima are 1.43030 mm apart; successive maxima on one side are 0.51436 mm apart.

cards.title: The common textbook approximation
cards.body: Using β ≈ 3π/2 and 5π/2 gives maxima at 0.750 and 1.250 mm. Then the symmetric first pair is 1.500 mm apart, or the first two on one side differ by 0.500 mm.

cards.title: Remember
points: State which two positions are meant before subtracting.
Minima are exact in sinθ; focal-plane positions here use the small-angle approximation.
Secondary maxima solve tanβ = β; half-integer multiples of π are approximate.

cards.q: Before calculating a separation, identify both ____.
cards.why: A coordinate measured from the centre is not itself a separation between two points.

cards.q: The half-integer rule for secondary maxima is ____.
cards.why: Exact noncentral maxima satisfy tanβ = β.

cards.q: The minima on opposite sides of the central maximum are ____.
cards.why: A uniformly illuminated slit gives an even intensity pattern in angle.

cards.title: Question 12
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Derive the expression for the resultant electric field and intensity distribution in the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern produced by two parallel slits, each of width \(b\) and separated by a distance \(d\). Show that when \(b=d\), the resulting diffraction pattern corresponds to that of a single slit of width \(2b\).
Did you define slit-centre spacing and obtain the single-slit field?

options.t: \(d\) is centre spacing; each slit contributes \(A_s\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\), with \(\beta\) defined
Correct field but geometry/parameters incomplete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The touching-slit limit \(b=d\) confirms the centre-spacing convention.

cards.q: Did you add fields before squaring?

options.t: Opposite \(\pm\gamma\) phases give field \(2A_s\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\cos\gamma\) and the correct intensity
Correct intensity quoted without field addition
Added intensities incoherently

cards.why: Coherent amplitudes interfere.

cards.q: Did you prove the \(b=d\) limit including its normalization?

options.t: \(\gamma=\beta\), the \(\sin2\beta\) identity, and \(4I_s[\sin(2\beta)/(2\beta)]^2\)
Correct limit asserted without the identity
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The joined aperture has width \(2b\) and twice the on-axis field.

cards.title: Two coherent slits, one focal plane
cards.body: The phase difference of slit-centre fields is 2γ = 2πd sinθ/λ. The lens brings parallel rays at angle θ to P; O is the central point.

cards.title: Aperture integral to two-slit intensity
cards.legend: k = 2π/λ; β = kb sinθ/2; γ = kd sinθ/2; A_s = ab is one slit's on-axis field. Slit centres lie at ±d/2.

steps.note: Fraunhofer field is the coherent aperture integral.
The symmetric integral gives the sinc factor.

ask.q: What must be added across the aperture?
ask.why: Different aperture points have phase differences.

steps.note: Translation of each slit adds its centre phase.
The centre phase difference is 2γ.

ask.q: What does d represent in γ?
ask.why: The relative centre phase is kd sinθ.

steps.note: Let I_s be proportional to |A_s|².

ask.q: Which factor is the single-slit envelope?
ask.why: It arises from integration within each slit.

steps.note: Now γ = β, and the two slits touch.
This is a width-2b slit with on-axis intensity 4I_s.

ask.q: What physical aperture remains when d = b?
ask.why: Centre spacing equal to slit width leaves no opaque gap.

cards.title: Fringes inside the slit envelope
cards.body: For d = 3b, the dotted curve is the single-slit envelope. The rapid fringes stay inside it; the third interference order is missing at the envelope zero. The plotted intensity is normalized.

cards.title: Remember
points: Integrate each slit field, then add the two centre phases.
Square only after adding fields.
When d = b, the aperture becomes a single opening of width 2b.

cards.q: The two slit fields must be added ____.
cards.why: Their stable relative phase causes interference.

cards.q: At d = b, the two openings ____.
cards.why: Their centre separation equals their width.

cards.q: The intensity is proportional to the field magnitude ____.
cards.why: Detected optical power is quadratic in field amplitude.

cards.title: Question 13
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: A diffraction grating having \(15{,}000\) lines per inch is illuminated normally by sodium light (\(\lambda_1=5890\,\mathrm{\AA}\) and \(\lambda_2=5896\,\mathrm{\AA}\)). Calculate: (i) the angular separation of the \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) lines in the second-order spectrum, and (ii) the linear separation between the two lines in the first-order spectrum observed on the focal plane of a convex lens of focal length \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\).
Did you convert the line density and wavelengths correctly?

options.t: Correct method with one unit error
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: An inch is 2.54 cm, and one ångström is 10⁻¹⁰ m.

cards.q: Did you obtain the second-order angular separation?

options.t: θ values about 44.0806° and 44.1371°; Δθ ≈ 0.00098697 rad = 3.393 arcmin
Correct differential dispersion method with minor rounding error
Used first order or confused radians and degrees

cards.why: Use order two for part (i), including cosθ in the dispersion.

cards.q: Did you use first order and state the focal-plane convention?

options.t: Conventional fΔθ ≈ 0.03780 mm with local-axis assumption, or normal-to-grating plane fΔtanθ ≈ 0.04300 mm stated
Correct first-order method with arithmetic error or unstated geometry
Used order two or a wrong length conversion

cards.why: The paper does not specify lens/screen orientation. A flat plane normal to the grating normal uses y = f tanθ.

cards.title: Convert the grating data
cards.body: Keep the two supplied wavelengths as λ₁ and λ₂. Their separation is independent of which sodium D label is assigned.

cards.title: Second-order angular result
cards.body: Angles are approximately 44.08058° and 44.13712°. The differential approximation 2Δλ/(d cosθ) at the mean wavelength gives the same rounded result.

cards.title: First-order local focal-plane result
cards.body: This is the conventional local linear-dispersion result with the lens/screen referenced to the mean diffracted beam. It also follows the usual y ≈ fθ treatment.

cards.title: If the focal plane is normal to the grating normal
cards.body: Here the first-order angles are about 20.35493° and 20.37658°. State the geometry; do not silently mix tanθ coordinates with fΔθ.

cards.title: Remember
points: Spacing is the reciprocal of line density after unit conversion.
Part (i) uses order two; part (ii) uses order one.
Angular differences in formulas for lengths must be in radians.
State whether the focal plane uses a local beam axis or the grating-normal axis.

cards.q: The grating spacing is the ____ of line density.
cards.why: Lines per metre invert to metres per line.

cards.q: The angle difference in fΔθ must be expressed in ____.
cards.why: The small-angle length relation assumes radian measure.

cards.q: The two parts of this question use ____ diffraction orders.
cards.why: They ask for second-order angles and first-order linear separation.

cards.title: Question 14
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: With a neat figure, explain the construction of Fresnel’s half-period zones on a plane wavefront. Show that the areas of all half-period zones are approximately equal to \(\pi\lambda d\), and prove that the resultant amplitude at an axial point due to the entire wavefront is half the amplitude produced by the first half-period zone.
Did you construct the zones using half-wavelength path increments?

options.t: Labelled wavefront, axial point at \(d\), and \(\sqrt{d^2+r_n^2}-d=n\lambda/2\)
Correct concentric zones but incomplete path construction
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Each successive zone has about a \(\pi\) phase shift relative to its neighbour.

cards.q: Did you obtain the approximate radius and equal annular areas?

options.t: \(r_n^2\approx n\lambda d\) and \(\pi(r_n^2-r_{n-1}^2)\approx\pi\lambda d\)
Radius formula only or disk area confused with zone area
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The paraxial approximation drops terms of order \(\lambda^2\).

cards.q: Did you justify the half-first-zone amplitude result?

options.t: Alternating zone sum, slowly varying contributions and grouped cancellation give \(A\approx a_1/2\)
Correct result quoted without cancellation argument
Confused amplitude half with intensity half

cards.why: The corresponding full-wavefront intensity is about one quarter of the isolated first-zone intensity.

cards.title: Concentric zones around the axis
cards.body: Draw circles on the plane wavefront centred at the axial foot O. At boundary n, the path to P exceeds OP by nλ/2. Successive annuli are the half-period zones.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Concentric Fresnel zones on a plane wavefront and paths to an axial point"><ellipse cx="60" cy="88" rx="40" ry="70" class="s ok"/><ellipse cx="60" cy="88" rx="32" ry="55" class="lk"/><ellipse cx="60" cy="88" rx="22" ry="39" class="lk"/><ellipse cx="60" cy="88" rx="13" ry="24" class="lk"/><path d="M60 88H232M60 18L232 88M60 49L232 88" class="lk"/><path d="M60 88V49" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><text x="43" y="94" class="t" font-size="12">O</text><text x="236" y="92" class="t" font-size="12">P</text><text x="138" y="107" class="t" font-size="12">d</text><text x="66" y="68" class="t" font-size="11">r_n</text><text x="108" y="31" class="t" font-size="11">d + nλ/2</text><text x="13" y="173" class="t" font-size="11">plane wavefront</text></svg>

cards.title: Path condition to equal zone areas
cards.legend: d is axial observation distance, r_n the nth boundary radius, λ much smaller than d.

steps.note: The nth boundary adds n half-wavelengths.
Square the path equation.

ask.q: Why are boundary paths spaced by λ/2?
options: To separate adjacent phases by π
ask.why: A path increment λ/2 is a half-period phase change.

steps.note: Remove the common axial-distance square.

ask.q: Which term is a small correction in the paraxial zone construction?
ask.why: It is small when the relevant nλ is much less than d.

steps.note: From here equality is within the leading paraxial approximation.
Within this approximation, subtract adjacent disk areas.

ask.q: What geometric area is a half-period zone?
ask.why: Only the first zone is a central disk.

steps.note: The leading approximate annular area is independent of n.

ask.q: What happens to the leading n dependence?
ask.why: Subtracting n−1 from n leaves one.

cards.title: Group the alternating zone fields
cards.body: The positive magnitudes a_n decrease slowly through distance/obliquity factors. Locally a₂ ≈ (a₁+a₃)/2 and similarly for later groups, making the brackets approximately cancel.

cards.title: Full-wavefront amplitude
cards.body: This is the Fresnel zone approximation for the unobstructed wavefront. Equal annular areas alone do not mean all zone amplitudes remain exactly equal forever.

cards.title: Remember
points: Construct zones by path difference, not equal radial widths.
Zone radii grow as √n; their areas are approximately equal.
Alternate phase signs cause cancellation.
Half amplitude implies quarter intensity.

cards.q: Successive zone boundary radii grow like the ____ root of the zone number.
cards.why: r_n² is proportional to n.

cards.q: The signs of successive zone contributions ____.
cards.why: Successive zones differ approximately by π in phase.

cards.q: The full-wavefront amplitude is approximately ____ the first-zone amplitude.
cards.why: Grouped alternating-zone contributions cancel apart from half the first term.

sheets.title: Q15 · Zone plate and its foci

cards.title: Question 15
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Explain the principle and construction of a Fresnel zone plate and show that it produces multiple foci. Consider a zone plate with radii \(r_n=0.1\sqrt n\,\mathrm{cm}\); for \(\lambda=5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}\), calculate the positions of the principal and secondary foci.
Did you explain alternate-zone transmission and the construction?

options.t: Concentric √n boundary radii and alternate opaque/transparent zones suppress cancellation
Construction or focusing principle only
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: At the design focus the selected zone contributions reinforce.

cards.q: Did you justify multiple odd-order positive foci?

options.t: Adjacent-zone phase becomes an odd multiple of π at f₁/(2k+1), so transmitted alternate zones reinforce
Odd focus formula quoted without explanation
Listed all integer orders as equal foci

cards.why: This is a conventional binary amplitude zone plate.

cards.q: Did you obtain the principal and secondary distances?

options.t: Correct principal focus only or correct method with a unit error
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Use r₁² = 0.01 cm² divided by λ in cm.

cards.title: An alternating ring mask
cards.body: Alternate Fresnel zones are made opaque. The remaining zones add with nearly the same phase at a focus; the mask sacrifices some light to avoid destructive cancellation.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Concentric alternating transmitting and opaque rings of a Fresnel zone plate"><circle cx="85" cy="85" r="68" class="f"/><circle cx="85" cy="85" r="60.8" class="s"/><circle cx="85" cy="85" r="52.7" class="f"/><circle cx="85" cy="85" r="43" class="s"/><circle cx="85" cy="85" r="30.4" class="f"/><path d="M85 85H153" class="hk" stroke-width="2"/><text x="163" y="79" class="t" font-size="12">r_n ∝ √n</text><text x="165" y="103" class="t" font-size="11">alternate zones</text><text x="25" y="171" class="t" font-size="11">Opaque and transmitting rings</text></svg>

cards.title: Why the positive foci are odd orders
cards.legend: Use paraxial plane-wave illumination and fixed radius r₁. Positive focusing orders are q = 1,3,5,… for this amplitude plate.

steps.note: The first boundary's paraxial excess path at distance z.
Convert path difference into phase.

ask.q: What converts optical path difference to phase?
ask.why: One wavelength corresponds to a full 2π phase.

steps.note: Take q odd, so alternating transmitted zones stay in phase.

ask.q: Which q values correspond to the converging amplitude-plate orders?
ask.why: The alternating transmission mask has odd-order focusing harmonics.

steps.note: Each allowed q gives another axial focus.

ask.q: How does focus distance change when q increases?
ask.why: q is in the denominator.

steps.note: Thus f₁, f₁/3, f₁/5, … are the positive foci.

ask.q: What is the first secondary positive focus?
ask.why: The next allowed positive odd order is three.

cards.title: Use centimetres consistently
cards.body: The focus f₇ is 28.57 cm, with further odd-order foci closer to the plate. These are distances for the specified wavelength.

cards.title: Remember
points: A zone plate selects alternate Fresnel zones.
The radius sequence is √n, not equally spaced radii.
The principal focus is 200 cm for these data.
Secondary positive foci occur at odd divisions of the principal distance.

cards.q: The transmitting rings select ____ zones.
cards.why: This prevents cancellation by adjacent opposite-phase contributions.

cards.q: The zone-plate focus depends on ____.
cards.why: Its diffractive phase condition contains λ.

cards.q: The secondary positive foci lie ____ to the plate than the principal focus.
cards.why: They are at f₁/3, f₁/5 and smaller distances.

cards.title: Question 16
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Obtain the expression for the intensity distribution on a screen due to Fresnel diffraction of a plane wave incident normally on a straight edge in terms of the Fresnel integrals \(C(v_0)\) and \(S(v_0)\). Hence show that the intensity on the edge of the geometrical shadow is \(\frac14I_0\).
Did you state the edge geometry and the Fresnel field integral?

options.t: Half-plane aperture, scaled lower limit v₀ and integral from v₀ to infinity
Correct integral without geometry or scaling
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A straight edge blocks one side of the incident wavefront.

cards.q: Did you normalize and obtain both squared Fresnel terms?

options.t: \(I/I_0=\tfrac12[(\tfrac12-C(v_0))^2+(\tfrac12-S(v_0))^2]\) with consistent sign convention
Correct structure with a normalization/sign inconsistency
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: \(I_0\) is the unobstructed intensity, not the edge intensity.

cards.q: Did you evaluate the shadow boundary?

options.t: \(v_0=0\), \(C=S=0\), so \(I=I_0/4\); correct illuminated/shadow limits
Quarter-intensity result without substitution
Claimed half intensity

cards.why: The field is halved at the boundary, so its squared magnitude is quartered.

cards.title: Choose the edge coordinate once
cards.body: Let y be positive into the geometrically illuminated region, with screen distance D. Then v₀ = −y√(2/λD). Negative v₀ is the bright side.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Straight edge and geometrical shadow on a screen with positive y on the lit side"><rect x="66" y="90" width="12" height="70" class="f"/><path d="M66 17V90M22 35H58M22 62H58M22 90H58M78 90H234M234 20V160" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M78 90L234 47" class="hk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M78 90L234 137" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><text x="239" y="47" class="t" font-size="11">P</text><text x="239" y="94" class="t" font-size="11">O</text><text x="149" y="113" class="t" font-size="11">shadow</text><text x="166" y="33" class="t" font-size="11">y > 0</text><text x="134" y="171" class="t" font-size="12">distance D</text></svg>

cards.title: Half-plane integral to the edge value
cards.legend: I₀ is unobstructed intensity. C and S use phase πv²/2; the full normalized integral is 1+j.

phases.name: Boundary
phases.why: put the lower limit at zero

steps.note: Normalize by the unobstructed full-line Fresnel integral.
Each integral from zero to positive infinity is one half.

ask.q: Why do the one-half constants appear?
options: They are the positive-infinity limits of C and S
ask.why: The integration runs from v₀ to infinity.

steps.note: The denominator is |1+j|².

ask.q: Why is the denominator two?
ask.why: Intensity is a squared field magnitude, including its normalization.

steps.note: Both Fresnel integrals vanish at zero.

ask.q: Which scaled coordinate is the geometrical boundary?
ask.why: y = 0 implies v₀ = 0.

steps.note: Half the field produces quarter the intensity.

ask.q: What does a factor one half in field amplitude do to intensity?
ask.why: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.

cards.title: Check both far-side limits
cards.body: Deep shadow corresponds to y negative; far into the lit side, the unobstructed intensity is recovered with damped fringes.

cards.title: Remember
points: Declare the sign of v₀ before using the Fresnel formula.
Normalize to the unobstructed intensity.
At the shadow edge the field is halved and intensity quartered.

cards.q: I₀ denotes the ____ intensity.
cards.why: The diffraction distribution is normalized to the beam without the edge.

cards.q: At the geometrical boundary, both Fresnel integrals ____.
cards.why: Their lower-to-upper integration interval has zero length at argument zero.

cards.q: The edge result is a ____ intensity.
cards.why: The half-amplitude field is squared.

cards.title: Question 17
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Draw the intensity distribution curve of Fresnel’s diffraction at a straight edge and explain its main features. Consider a straight edge illuminated by a parallel beam of light with \(\lambda=6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}\); calculate the positions of the first two maxima and the first minimum on a screen at a distance of \(50\,\mathrm{cm}\) from the edge (given \(v_0=-1.22,-2.34\) for the first two maxima and \(v_0=-1.87\) for the first minimum).
Did you draw and explain the asymmetric edge pattern?

options.t: Quarter intensity at edge, monotonic shadow decay, damped lit-side fringes about I₀
Only some features correctly shown
Symmetric slit pattern or no graph

cards.why: The first lit-side maximum reaches approximately 1.37 I₀.

cards.q: Did you set the coordinate scale with a consistent sign?

options.t: \(y=-v_0\sqrt{\lambda D/2}\), scale \(\approx0.38730\,\mathrm{mm}\), positive \(y\) into light
Correct magnitude scale but sign or units unclear
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The given negative \(v_0\) values all lie on the illuminated side.

cards.q: Did you obtain all three positions?

options.t: Maxima at +0.4725 and +0.9063 mm; first minimum at +0.7242 mm
One or two correct positions
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The first minimum lies between the first two maxima.

cards.title: The straight-edge intensity curve
cards.body: The edge is at y = 0. Intensity there is I₀/4; the first lit-side peak is about 1.37 I₀. Later oscillations settle towards I₀, while the shadow intensity decays towards zero.

cards.title: One length scale for all three
cards.body: Use centimetres consistently before converting the result to millimetres.

cards.title: Insert the supplied Fresnel coordinates
cards.body: All are positive into the illuminated side because y = −v₀√(λD/2). They are measured from the geometrical shadow boundary, not from the first maximum.

cards.title: Remember
points: The edge pattern is asymmetric.
The sign convention maps negative v₀ to the illuminated side.
The first minimum falls between the first two maxima.
Screen distances scale as √(λD).

cards.q: The bright-side oscillations eventually approach the ____ intensity.
cards.why: Far from the edge the wave behaves like the unobstructed beam.

cards.q: The supplied negative Fresnel coordinates lie on the ____ side.
The first minimum lies ____ the first two maxima.
cards.why: 0.724 mm lies between 0.473 mm and 0.906 mm.

cards.title: Question 18
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: With suitable diagrams, explain how the experiment with transverse waves on a string passing through two narrow slits and the corresponding optical experiment with two Polaroids demonstrate the transverse wave nature of light. Why cannot longitudinal waves exhibit polarization?
Did you explain the string-and-slits experiment?

options.t: First slit selects a transverse vibration plane; parallel second slit passes it, crossed second slit blocks it
Correct parallel/crossed observation without the selection argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The slit constrains the allowed direction of transverse string motion.

cards.q: Did you explain the corresponding two-Polaroid observations with diagrams?

options.t: First polarizer selects E direction; parallel axes transmit, crossed ideal axes extinguish
Observations correct but diagram or E-direction explanation incomplete
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Rotating the analyser changes transmission according to a transverse direction.

cards.q: Did you explain the conclusion and longitudinal contrast?

options.t: Direction selection proves transverse oscillations; longitudinal motion has no independent transverse vibration directions to select
Correct conclusion without the physical contrast
Claimed ordinary sound polarizes in the same way

cards.why: For a longitudinal wave the displacement is parallel to travel, so rotation about that direction supplies no new displacement orientation.

cards.title: Slits select a string vibration plane
cards.body: With both narrow slits aligned to the vibration plane, the wave passes. Rotate the second slit through 90°: that transverse motion is blocked.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="String vibration passes parallel slit selectors and is blocked by a crossed selector"><path d="M12 48H242M12 128H242M75 22V74M166 22V74M75 102V154M143 128H195" class="gk"/><path d="M12 48q12-22 24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0M12 128q12-22 24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0t24 0" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M174 118L191 137M191 118L174 137" class="hk" stroke-width="2"/><text x="198" y="28" class="t" font-size="11">passes</text><text x="201" y="150" class="t" font-size="11">blocked</text><text x="13" y="175" class="t" font-size="11">Travel →; vibration up/down</text></svg>

cards.title: Polaroids make the optical test
cards.body: The first Polaroid selects one electric-field direction. A parallel analyser transmits it; an ideal crossed analyser extinguishes it. Real elements can leak a small amount.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Two Polaroids with parallel transmission axes pass light, crossed axes extinguish it"><path d="M15 50H244M15 128H244" class="gk"/><rect x="64" y="20" width="35" height="60" class="s ok"/><rect x="166" y="20" width="35" height="60" class="s ok"/><rect x="64" y="98" width="35" height="60" class="s ok"/><rect x="166" y="98" width="35" height="60" class="s ok"/><path d="M81 26V74M184 26V74M81 104V152M171 128H196" class="lk" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M109 36V65" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><text x="210" y="54" class="t" font-size="11">light</text><text x="210" y="132" class="t" font-size="11">dark</text><text x="69" y="174" class="t" font-size="11">P</text><text x="173" y="174" class="t" font-size="11">A</text></svg>

cards.title: Why ordinary longitudinal waves differ
cards.body: A longitudinal displacement is parallel to propagation. There are no two independent transverse displacement directions for an axis selector to choose, so this polarization test cannot occur.

cards.title: Remember
points: Selection of one vibration direction is the core observation.
Use parallel and crossed selectors in both experiments.
For light it is the electric-field direction that is selected.
Ordinary longitudinal waves lack the independent transverse directions needed for this test.

cards.q: Crossed ideal polarizers cause ____.
cards.why: The first selected electric field has no component along the crossed analyser axis.

cards.q: Polarization demonstrates that light is ____.
cards.why: Its oscillations have a selectable direction perpendicular to travel.

cards.q: The second Polaroid acts as the ____.
cards.why: It tests the state prepared by the first polarizer.

sections.title: Section C · 10 marks each · best one

cards.title: Question 19
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: Discuss the Fraunhofer type of diffraction produced by a narrow single slit illuminated normally by monochromatic light. Derive the expression for the intensity distribution, obtain the conditions for maxima and minima, explain the graphical method for finding the positions of secondary maxima, and draw a diagram indicating the intensity distribution in the diffraction pattern.
Did you give the geometry and the coherent aperture integral?

options.t: Plane normal incidence, width b, lens focal screen, path x sinθ and field integral
Correct set-up without a complete field construction
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A Fraunhofer field adds contributions with a phase linear in aperture position.

cards.q: Did you derive and normalize the intensity distribution?

options.t: \(A=A_0\sin\beta/\beta\), \(I=I_0(\sin\beta/\beta)^2\), \(\beta=\pi b\sin\theta/\lambda\)
Correct final formula without integration or parameter definition
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: At \(\beta=0\), use the sinc limit to obtain \(I_0\).

cards.q: Did you state the minima and central width?

options.t: \(b\sin\theta=m\lambda\), nonzero integer \(m\); central angular width \(\approx2\lambda/b\)
Only minima or width correct
Counted the central maximum as a zero

cards.why: The central maximum is between the first zeros on opposite sides.

cards.q: Did you derive the secondary-maxima condition and explain its graphical solution?

options.t: Differentiate intensity, get \(\tan\beta=\beta\), intersections of \(y=\tan\beta\) and \(y=\beta\), with roots about 4.493 and 7.725
Correct condition without graphical construction or roots
Used \(\beta=(m+\tfrac12)\pi\) as an exact law

cards.why: The nonzero intersections give secondary maxima; exclude minima and the removable centre.

cards.q: Did you draw and describe the true intensity pattern?

options.t: Symmetric bright broad centre, zero minima, weak secondary peaks of decreasing height
Qualitative sketch missing quantitative features
Only a two-slit fringe pattern or no graph

cards.why: The first two secondary peak intensities are approximately 4.72% and 1.65% of the centre.

cards.title: Slit, lens and screen
cards.body: A plane wave illuminates width b uniformly. A lens maps rays at angle θ to screen point P. The centre O receives the θ = 0 contributions in phase.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Single-slit Fraunhofer set-up with aperture width b, ray angle theta, lens and focal screen"><path d="M50 15V53M50 119V160M18 37H43M18 86H43M18 142H43M140 15V162M233 15V162M51 55L140 41L233 48M51 118L140 104L233 48M51 55L140 55L233 87M51 118L140 118L233 87" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M140 15c-14 34-14 113 0 147c14-34 14-113 0-147M51 55H94L51 118" class="gk"/><path d="M62 55V118" class="hk" stroke-width="2"/><text x="66" y="92" class="t" font-size="12">b</text><text x="79" y="32" class="t" font-size="11">θ</text><text x="237" y="51" class="t" font-size="12">P</text><text x="237" y="91" class="t" font-size="12">O</text><text x="16" y="176" class="t" font-size="11">slit</text><text x="128" y="176" class="t" font-size="11">lens</text><text x="199" y="176" class="t" font-size="11">screen</text></svg>

cards.title: Single-slit field and stationary intensity
cards.legend: a is field per unit slit width; β = πb sinθ/λ; A₀ = ab. Take uniformly coherent aperture illumination.

steps.note: The path difference from coordinate x is x sinθ.
The two symmetric endpoints give a sine.
Normalize I₀ to the on-axis intensity.

ask.q: Why is the field, rather than intensity, integrated?
ask.why: The relative phases determine constructive and destructive interference.

steps.note: This expression is used for β nonzero.

ask.q: Which quantity is differentiated to locate angular extrema?
options: Intensity as a function of β
ask.why: At fixed b and λ, β parametrizes the diffraction angle.

steps.note: Zeros of sinβ are minima; the other factor gives secondary maxima.

ask.q: Which roots correspond to noncentral minima?
ask.why: The sinc numerator vanishes there while its denominator is nonzero.

steps.note: Select the other stationary-point factor.
Nonzero roots give the secondary maxima.

ask.q: Which graphical construction finds these roots?
ask.why: The solutions make the two function values equal.

cards.title: Minima and central width
cards.body: The width formulas are paraxial. The exact angular central width, when the first zeros exist, is 2 arcsin(λ/b).

cards.title: Graphical roots of tanβ = β
cards.body: Plot y = tanβ with separate branches and y = β. Nonzero intersections give β ≈ ±4.4934, ±7.7253, …. The poles at half-integer π are not roots.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Schematic intersection of a tangent branch and the line y equals beta, before the tangent pole"><path d="M25 148H242M25 148V15M212 18V148" class="gk" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><path d="M25 148L235 28" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M121 148C160 143 180 91 192 53C198 35 202 23 204 16" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="192" cy="53" r="4" class="h"/><text x="35" y="30" class="t" font-size="12">y = tan β</text><text x="81" y="80" class="t" font-size="12">y = β</text><text x="143" y="112" class="t" font-size="11">nonzero root</text><text x="196" y="168" class="t" font-size="11">pole</text><text x="28" y="168" class="t" font-size="11">schematic branch</text></svg>

cards.title: The normalized single-slit pattern
cards.body: The central maximum is twice the angular width of each neighbouring lobe between minima. The first two side peaks are about 4.72% and 1.65% of I₀.

cards.title: Remember
points: Fraunhofer field comes from the coherent aperture integral.
β = 0 uses a limit and is the main maximum.
Nonzero integer π gives minima; tanβ = β gives secondary maxima.
The half-integer rule for side maxima is approximate.
Narrower slit means wider angular central maximum.

cards.q: The central sinc value is evaluated using a ____.
cards.why: sinβ/β tends to one as β tends to zero.

cards.q: The first secondary peaks are much ____ than the centre.
cards.why: Their intensities are only about 4.72% of I₀.

cards.q: Reducing slit width makes the central angular peak ____.
cards.why: The central angular width is approximately 2λ/b.

sheets.title: Q20 · N slits and sharp maxima

cards.title: Question 20
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: Derive the expression for the intensity distribution in Fraunhofer diffraction due to \(N\) identical parallel slits. Discuss the positions of principal maxima, secondary minima, and absent spectra, and derive the equation for the angular half-width of the principal maxima to show that they become sharper as \(N\) increases.
Did you define the geometry and sum N coherent slit fields?

options.t: Width b, centre spacing d, equal fields with phase step 2γ, geometric-series sum
Correct set-up or sum without a full derivation
Added intensities without phases

cards.why: The geometric sum gives the N-slit interference factor.

cards.q: Did you obtain the full intensity including the envelope?

options.t: \(I=I_s(\sin\beta/\beta)^2[\sin(N\gamma)/\sin\gamma]^2\), with \(\beta,\gamma\) defined
Only interference factor or missing normalization
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Finite slit width cannot be omitted when discussing absent spectra.

cards.q: Did you state principal maxima and secondary minima correctly?

options.t: \(\gamma=m\pi\) principal maxima with limiting factor \(N^2\); \(\gamma=p\pi/N\), excluding multiples of \(N\), for minima
Only one set correct
Counted \(0/0\) principal maxima as minima

cards.why: There are \(N-1\) interference minima between adjacent principal orders.

cards.q: Did you give the condition for absent spectra?

options.t: \(d\sin\theta=m\lambda\) and \(b\sin\theta=q\lambda\), \(q\ne0\), so \(mb=qd\)
Envelope cancellation explained without equations
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A principal interference maximum is absent if its envelope is zero.

cards.q: Did you derive angular half-width and explain sharpening?

options.t: Nearest zero has \(\Delta\gamma=\pi/N\); \(\delta\theta\approx\lambda/(Nd\cos\theta_m)\), so width decreases as \(1/N\)
Correct width formula without the nearest-zero argument
Confused full width, half width and half-power width

cards.why: This half-width is maximum-to-first-zero, not the half-maximum width.

cards.title: A regularly spaced slit array
cards.body: Each slit contributes its own sinc field. Translation by centre spacing d adds a phase step 2γ. A lens maps the common outgoing angle to P on the focal screen.

cards.title: Geometric field sum and first-zero width
cards.legend: β = πb sinθ/λ, γ = πd sinθ/λ, A₁ = A_s sinβ/β. Equal slit illumination; irrelevant overall phase drops out of intensity.

steps.note: Start from the N coherent slit fields.
Use the finite geometric series.

ask.q: Why is a geometric series appropriate?
options: Adjacent slit fields have a constant phase ratio
ask.why: Each shift by d multiplies the field by e^{j2γ}.

steps.note: Separate a pure phase from the real interference ratio.
The overall phase has unit magnitude.

ask.q: What survives squaring from the pure exponential phase?

steps.note: All slit-centre phasors align; use the limiting ratio N.

ask.q: What is the interference intensity factor at γ = mπ?
ask.why: Both sine terms vanish, but their field ratio tends in magnitude to N.

steps.note: The nearest numerator zeros flank the principal maximum.
Linearize sinθ; from here equality uses the narrow-peak approximation.
Approximate first-zero half-width: increasing N sharpens the peak.

ask.q: Which width does this formula describe?
ask.why: It was obtained from the first numerator zero on either side.

cards.title: Count the extrema correctly
cards.body: Between adjacent principal interference maxima there are N−1 minima and N−2 weak secondary maxima. The finite-slit envelope can suppress peaks and shift total-pattern extrema.

cards.title: Absent spectra and width conventions
cards.body: The absent-order condition combines a grating maximum with a noncentral slit minimum. The full first-zero width is twice the half-width; it is not the full width at half maximum.

cards.title: Four-slit interference factor
cards.body: This is the normalized interference factor for N = 4, before multiplying the slit envelope. Between adjacent principal maxima there are three zeros and two weak secondary peaks.

cards.title: Remember
points: Sum N phased fields as a geometric series.
Principal orders satisfy d sinθ = mλ and have an N² interference factor.
Exclude multiples of N when counting the pπ/N minima.
Envelope zeros can remove principal orders.
First-zero angular half-width falls as 1/N at fixed slit spacing and order.

cards.q: Increasing the illuminated slit count makes principal maxima ____.
cards.why: Their first-zero angular half-width is inversely proportional to N.

cards.q: A principal order disappears when the slit envelope ____.
cards.why: Zero times the N-slit interference factor still gives zero intensity.

cards.q: The N-slit field sum is a finite ____ series.
cards.why: Successive terms have the same complex phase ratio.
